editorial_title_zh: 温柔的痛楚：一个可供栖居的身体
editorial_excerpt_zh: 受苦的拥抱：Angelo Madsen 的长片纪录片《一个可供栖居的身体》与 Tiona Nekkia McClodden 的录像装置，以柔和而专注的视角探索施虐受虐
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在 Angelo Madsen 关于已故身体改造传奇 Fakir Musafar 的纪录片《一个可供栖居的身体》（A Body to Live In，2025）接近结尾处，Musafar 与他的妻子、女施虐者 Cléo DuBois 为 Fakir 的情人 William “Grin” Grindatti 进行了一场悬挂仪式。Grin 身上布满穿刺与纹身，身形远高于两人娇小的身躯，却对这一行为出奇地焦虑。尽管如此，他还是照做了。Fakir 让针穿过 Grin 背部的皮肉，如同一把热刀切过黄油。随后他将钩子插入 Grin 的皮肤，钩子通过钢夹连接到架子上，缓缓将他拉向空中。Fakir 握住他的手，引导他呼吸以使他平静。Grin 的眼中开始涌出泪水。没有人说话。房间里充满情感张力。当 Fakir 示意 Cléo 把 Grin 放下来时，Cléo 很快也哭了。我意识到，我也哭了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "也许当今高度媒介化文化最具破坏性的后果之一，是人们越来越习惯于透过纯粹视觉的镜头来看待电影（尤其是强调性与暴力的作品）——从而将其与自身的情感层面割裂开来。与这一倾向相对，由 kink 亚文化成员创作的当代施虐受虐或欲望政治探索，如《一个可供栖居的身体》和 Tiona Nekkia McClodden 的录像装置，邀请观众以更温柔、更专注的视角去体验身体暴力。McClodden 的作品描绘了她对施虐行为的臣服，同时明确指涉国家与系统性暴力如何既塑造了她自己构建的臣服场景，又与之截然不同。但两位艺术家都没有采取调查式的方法；相反，两人都践行了学者 Avgi Saketopoulou 所说的“迫切施虐”（exigent sadism），其中暴力以某种程度的不透明性呈现。这类施虐不提供答案，而是为透过痛苦去看所涌现的一切留出空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管 Musafar（于 2018 年去世）一生都在试图定位他及其追随者行为的起源——他们追求痛苦的 raison d’être——Madsen 却避免给出任何单一确定的解释。《一个可供栖居的身体》从 DuBois 的个人档案中取材，包括照片、家庭录像、信件、电视出镜录像带等，记录了对这一切“为什么”的许多不同回答，Musafar 社群中一些 S/M 参与者提到通过自我施加的痛苦来追求能动性、完整与疗愈。这些参与者的叙述——他们投身 S/M 以应对施加于其人格的暴力——在情感上的清晰令人动容，比如 DuBois 所述在年轻时被强奸后想要重新夺回对自己身体的控制。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但更有趣的是那些无法为自己的施虐受虐倾向找到答案或理由的人，而 Madsen 保持并聚焦于他们的不透明感。Musafar 就是这样一个对象。例如，我们并未获得他生平的线性或编年式叙述，也没有看到他如何塑造 Fakir Musafar 这一人格——这个名字是他在 1970 年代正式采用的。我们透过他早期为镜头进行仪式表演时拍摄的照片，瞥见他在 1940 年代南达科他州作为一个非规范男孩的开端。当我们看到他青春期的黑白自拍——他穿着束身衣，身上布满晾衣夹——Musafar 在旁白中回忆起他进入限制实践的入门经历：十几岁时某个周末被独自留在家中，他禁食，用皮带束紧腰部，四处跳舞直到几乎昏厥，偶尔用相机记录下这场表演。整部影片中，我们看到 Musafar、DuBois 和他们的朋友从事 S/M 行为的类似照片。这些高对比度的图像占据画面和我们的凝视，感觉像是无限长的时间，但其实只有短短几秒。这些照片的静止令我们不安，因为它们只是偶尔配有轶事，关于这些痛苦行为——比如 DuBois 被乳房悬吊在空中——如何发生，几乎没有上下文。这种形式手法正是 Madsen 自己的施虐在起作用，迫使我们与如此多缺乏解答的图像和叙述共处。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《一个可供栖居的身体》让我想起 McClodden 的 90 分钟录像装置《The Brad Johnson Tape》（2017），其中这位电影人为已故美国黑人同性恋诗人的 10 首诗各表演一场 S/M 场景，既呼应又对抗 Johnson 写作中丰沛的酷儿情欲。录像的最后一部分以 Johnson 的《On Subjugation》（1988）为背景，McClodden 被脚倒挂在定制架子上。录像以低保真 VHS 拍摄，这意味着我们无法清楚看到她的面部表情，但能听到她因倒置压垮身体、挣扎着念完诗时急促的叹息与呼吸。只有设置为自动变焦的摄像机作为见证者，McClodden 的行为让人想起 Musafar 年轻时的自拍：两位艺术家都把相机当作一种替身，使他们能够将征服他人的意志转向自身。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《论征服》是约翰逊对体制如何将边缘化人群困住、使其成为帝国暴力的马前卒的批判——萨凯托普卢借用乔治·巴塔耶关于法西斯主义与施虐倾向的论述，将之称为“破坏性施虐”。约翰逊写道：“我用铁手套写作，你看不出来吗？已经采取了限制性措施，以确保一切表达都被扼杀。你无需害怕爱会毫无阻碍、如腹泻般奔涌而出。铁手套配铁腕国家！”这首诗很可能受到约翰逊在海军服役经历的影响，它提出了一个恰切的论点：国家制造出种种条件，使种族化人群与酷儿人群为服务于它而自我征服。这正是体面政治的计划：它将边缘化的身体设定为“问题”，以便让他们实施某种自我审查，试图成为模范公民。换言之，这是一种针对黑人生活的S/M。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "转向S/M是摆脱那些体面束缚的一条出路，正如麦克洛登所说：“参与BDSM可以让人体验到那种在发生之前就仿佛迫在眉睫的暴力……多年前我意识到，作为一名黑人酷儿女性，我可以用自己的手、通过S/M来满足这些冲动。我感兴趣的是合意之痛作为一种使身体变柔、变软，或触及内在自我的方式。”对于那些在生活中经历过破坏性施虐的人（无论是国家之手还是人际情境中），S/M提供了场所，将具身化的恐惧转化为别的东西，使他们得以越过暴力的时刻。现实是，我们都有能力伤害他人，而且我们常常在几乎没有或完全没有伤害意图的情况下这样做——只是单纯的粗心。目睹一个人为正在被自己身体伤害的人留出空间并施行事后照护，扰乱了我们的感官，也扰乱了我们对施害者与受难者的二元理解。看到对暴力的温柔拥抱，让我们得以领会打破这一动态会是什么样子。这是被以关怀承接的冲突。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这类作品常被用“夺回”“恢复”或“疗愈”之类新自由主义的陈词滥调来描述，而这些说法遮蔽了我们在身体与电影体验中那些更为未知的情感层面。这些导演将时间呈现为某种被感受的东西，而非被测量或控制的东西。通过抵制那种想要“完成”身体或恢复身体的疗愈主张，马德森和麦克洛登让我们成为共谋的窥视者，去窥看他们作为电影创作者以及他们的观众，在追求 exigent sadism 行为时，自身会变成什么。麦克洛登《论征服》段落的最后时刻，显示她喘息起伏，努力在录像带用完之前完成这首诗；她正通过及时完成这首诗，在身体上和美学上都接近一种 jouissance 状态。同样，在《A Body to Live In》中，穆萨法尔和杜布瓦通过与格林达蒂分享他们正施加于他的疼痛的时间状态，与他建立联结。在我看来，这就是一种虔诚电影的感觉——这种电影通过邀请我们温柔而关切地与他人共度时间、共同承受疼痛，让我们得以触碰自身内部的未知。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Toward the end of Angelo Madsen’s documentary about the late body-modification legend Fakir Musafar, A Body to Live In (2025), Musafar and his wife, dominatrix Cléo DuBois, perform a suspension ritual on Fakir’s lover William “Grin” Grindatti. Grin, who is covered in numerous piercings and tattoos, and towers over both of their petite frames, is surprisingly anxious about the act. Nonetheless, he goes through with it. Fakir glides a needle through the flesh on Grin’s back like a hot knife slicing through butter. He then inserts into Grin’s skin hooks that attach to a rack via a steel clip, and slowly pulls him into the air. Fakir holds his hands and guides him through his breathing to calm him. Tears begin to well up in Grin’s eyes. Nothing is said. The room is affectively charged. Cléo is soon crying as Fakir motions for her to bring Grin back down. I realize that I am, too."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Perhaps one of the most damaging outcomes of today’s hyper-mediated culture is that people are increasingly primed to view cinema (especially works that emphasize sex and violence) through a purely ocular lens—therefore unlinking it from its affective register. Countering this tendency, contemporary explorations of sadomasochism or the politics of desire made by members of kink subcultures, like A Body to Live In and Tiona Nekkia McClodden’s video installations, invite audiences to experience bodily violence through a more tender and attentive lens. McClodden’s work depicts her submission to sadist actions while making explicit references to how state and systemic violence both inform and vastly differ from her self-crafted scenes of subjugation. But neither artist pursues an investigative approach; instead, both enact what scholar Avgi Saketopoulou describes as “exigent sadism,” in which violence is presented with a certain degree of opacity. This type of sadism does not provide answers, but holds space for whatever emerges from the pursuit of seeing the pain through."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Though Musafar, who passed away in 2018, spent his life trying to locate the origin of his and his followers’ actions—their raison d’être for pursuing pain—Madsen steers away from providing any one definitive explanation. A Body to Live In is culled from DuBois’s personal archive of photographs, home movies, letters, taped televisual appearances, and more, and it documents many different replies to the why of it all, with some participants in S/M from Musafar’s community invoking the pursuit of agency, wholeness, and healing through self-administered pain. These accounts, of participants who took to S/M to grapple with the violence inflicted on their personhood, are moving in their emotional clarity—like DuBois’s stated desire to recuperate control over her body after being raped in her youth."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But more interesting are those who fail to arrive at answers or reasonings for their proclivity for sadomasochism, and Madsen maintains and centers their sense of opacity. Musafar is one such subject. We are not given any linear or chronological account of his life, for example, or a sense of how he crafted the persona of Fakir Musafar, a name he formally adopted in the 1970s. We glimpse his beginnings as a nonnormative boy in South Dakota in the 1940s through the pictures he took of his early ritual performances for the camera. As we see his adolescent black-and-white self-portraits, in which he’s dressed in corsets with clothespins all over his body, Musafar recalls in voiceover his initiation into the practice of restriction: left alone at home one weekend when he was a teenager, he fasted, cinched his waist with belts, and danced around until he almost passed out, occasionally documenting the performance with his camera. Throughout the film, we see similar photos of Musafar, DuBois, and their friends engaged in S/M acts. These high-contrast images hold the frame and our gaze for what feels like an infinite amount of time but is only mere seconds. The stillness of these pictures unnerves us, as they are only occasionally accompanied by anecdotes, with minimal context as to how these painful acts, like DuBois suspended in the air by her breasts, came to be. This formal approach is Madsen’s own sadism in action, forcing us to sit with so many images and narratives that lack resolution."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A Body to Live In brought to my mind McClodden’s 90-minute video installation The Brad Johnson Tape (2017), in which the filmmaker reads 10 poems by the late gay Black American poet while performing an S/M scene for each, playing with and against the lush queer erotics of Johnson’s writing. The final section of the video, set to Johnson’s “On Subjugation” (1988), sees McClodden suspended upside down from her feet in a custom-built rig. The video is shot on lo-fi VHS, which means that we cannot see her facial expressions very clearly, but we can hear her exasperated sighs and breaths as the inversion overwhelms her body and she struggles to finish the poem. With only the video camera, set to auto-zoom, operating as witness, McClodden’s act is reminiscent of Musafar’s self-portraits from his youth: both artists use the camera as a kind of body double that allows them to turn their will to subjugate others toward themselves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“On Subjugation” is Johnson’s critique of how institutions ensnare marginalized people and make them foot soldiers for its imperial violence—what Saketopoulou, drawing from Georges Bataille’s work on fascism and sadism, terms “destructive sadism.” Johnson writes, “AM WRITING WITH AN IRON GLOVE, CAN’T YOU TELL? RESTRICTIVE MEASURES HAVE BEEN TAKEN TO ENSURE THE STIFLING OF ALL EXPRESSION. YOU NEED FEAR NO EFFUSIVE BURGEONINGS OF UNIMPEDED AND DIARRHETIC RAMBLINGS FROM LOVE. IRON GLOVES FOR AN IRON STATE!” The poem was likely influenced by Johnson’s time in the Navy, and it makes the apt argument that the state creates conditions wherein racialized and queer people subjugate themselves in service to it. This is the project of respectability politics: it situates marginalized bodies as “problems” so that they enact a form of self-censure in an attempt to become exemplary citizens. It is, in other words, a type of S/M over Black life."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The turn to S/M is a way out from those respectable restraints, as McClodden says: “Engaging within BDSM can allow one to experience violence that may feel imminent before it happens . . . I realized years ago that I could satisfy these urges with my own hand, through S/M, as a Black queer woman. I was interested in consensual pain as a form of tenderizing, or softness, or something that is of the interior self.” For individuals who have experienced destructive sadism in their lives (either at the hands of the state or in interpersonal contexts), S/M offers sites to transform embodied fear into something else that allows them to move past the moment of violence. The reality is that we are all capable of harming others, and we often do so with little or no harmful intent—just simple carelessness. Witnessing someone hold space and perform aftercare for someone they are physically harming troubles our senses and our binary understanding of perpetrators and sufferers. Seeing tender embraces of violence allows us to grasp what breaches of this dynamic look like. It is conflict held with care."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Such works are often described using the neoliberal platitudes of reclaiming, recovery, or healing that obscure the more unknown affective registers of our experiences of both the body and cinema. These directors render time as something felt rather than measured or controlled. By resisting the claim of healing that desires to “complete” the body or restore it, Madsen and McClodden make us complicit voyeurs in their desire to see what becomes of themselves, as filmmakers, and their audiences when acts of exigent sadism are pursued. The final moments of McClodden’s “On Subjugation” segment show her panting and heaving as she struggles to finish the poem before the tape runs out; she is approaching a state of jouissance both physically and aesthetically by completing the poem in time. Likewise, in A Body to Live In , Musafar and DuBois bond with Grindatti by sharing with him the temporal state of pain they’re inflicting on him. This, to me, is what a cinema of devotion feels like—a cinema that, by inviting us to share time tenderly and caringly with others enduring pain, allows us to touch the unknown within ourselves."}]
article_text:
Toward the end of Angelo Madsen’s documentary about the late body-modification legend Fakir Musafar, A Body to Live In (2025), Musafar and his wife, dominatrix Cléo DuBois, perform a suspension ritual on Fakir’s lover William “Grin” Grindatti. Grin, who is covered in numerous piercings and tattoos, and towers over both of their petite frames, is surprisingly anxious about the act. Nonetheless, he goes through with it. Fakir glides a needle through the flesh on Grin’s back like a hot knife slicing through butter. He then inserts into Grin’s skin hooks that attach to a rack via a steel clip, and slowly pulls him into the air. Fakir holds his hands and guides him through his breathing to calm him. Tears begin to well up in Grin’s eyes. Nothing is said. The room is affectively charged. Cléo is soon crying as Fakir motions for her to bring Grin back down. I realize that I am, too.

Perhaps one of the most damaging outcomes of today’s hyper-mediated culture is that people are increasingly primed to view cinema (especially works that emphasize sex and violence) through a purely ocular lens—therefore unlinking it from its affective register. Countering this tendency, contemporary explorations of sadomasochism or the politics of desire made by members of kink subcultures, like A Body to Live In and Tiona Nekkia McClodden’s video installations, invite audiences to experience bodily violence through a more tender and attentive lens. McClodden’s work depicts her submission to sadist actions while making explicit references to how state and systemic violence both inform and vastly differ from her self-crafted scenes of subjugation. But neither artist pursues an investigative approach; instead, both enact what scholar Avgi Saketopoulou describes as “exigent sadism,” in which violence is presented with a certain degree of opacity. This type of sadism does not provide answers, but holds space for whatever emerges from the pursuit of seeing the pain through.

Though Musafar, who passed away in 2018, spent his life trying to locate the origin of his and his followers’ actions—their raison d’être for pursuing pain—Madsen steers away from providing any one definitive explanation. A Body to Live In is culled from DuBois’s personal archive of photographs, home movies, letters, taped televisual appearances, and more, and it documents many different replies to the why of it all, with some participants in S/M from Musafar’s community invoking the pursuit of agency, wholeness, and healing through self-administered pain. These accounts, of participants who took to S/M to grapple with the violence inflicted on their personhood, are moving in their emotional clarity—like DuBois’s stated desire to recuperate control over her body after being raped in her youth.

But more interesting are those who fail to arrive at answers or reasonings for their proclivity for sadomasochism, and Madsen maintains and centers their sense of opacity. Musafar is one such subject. We are not given any linear or chronological account of his life, for example, or a sense of how he crafted the persona of Fakir Musafar, a name he formally adopted in the 1970s. We glimpse his beginnings as a nonnormative boy in South Dakota in the 1940s through the pictures he took of his early ritual performances for the camera. As we see his adolescent black-and-white self-portraits, in which he’s dressed in corsets with clothespins all over his body, Musafar recalls in voiceover his initiation into the practice of restriction: left alone at home one weekend when he was a teenager, he fasted, cinched his waist with belts, and danced around until he almost passed out, occasionally documenting the performance with his camera. Throughout the film, we see similar photos of Musafar, DuBois, and their friends engaged in S/M acts. These high-contrast images hold the frame and our gaze for what feels like an infinite amount of time but is only mere seconds. The stillness of these pictures unnerves us, as they are only occasionally accompanied by anecdotes, with minimal context as to how these painful acts, like DuBois suspended in the air by her breasts, came to be. This formal approach is Madsen’s own sadism in action, forcing us to sit with so many images and narratives that lack resolution.

A Body to Live In brought to my mind McClodden’s 90-minute video installation The Brad Johnson Tape (2017), in which the filmmaker reads 10 poems by the late gay Black American poet while performing an S/M scene for each, playing with and against the lush queer erotics of Johnson’s writing. The final section of the video, set to Johnson’s “On Subjugation” (1988), sees McClodden suspended upside down from her feet in a custom-built rig. The video is shot on lo-fi VHS, which means that we cannot see her facial expressions very clearly, but we can hear her exasperated sighs and breaths as the inversion overwhelms her body and she struggles to finish the poem. With only the video camera, set to auto-zoom, operating as witness, McClodden’s act is reminiscent of Musafar’s self-portraits from his youth: both artists use the camera as a kind of body double that allows them to turn their will to subjugate others toward themselves.

“On Subjugation” is Johnson’s critique of how institutions ensnare marginalized people and make them foot soldiers for its imperial violence—what Saketopoulou, drawing from Georges Bataille’s work on fascism and sadism, terms “destructive sadism.” Johnson writes, “AM WRITING WITH AN IRON GLOVE, CAN’T YOU TELL? RESTRICTIVE MEASURES HAVE BEEN TAKEN TO ENSURE THE STIFLING OF ALL EXPRESSION. YOU NEED FEAR NO EFFUSIVE BURGEONINGS OF UNIMPEDED AND DIARRHETIC RAMBLINGS FROM LOVE. IRON GLOVES FOR AN IRON STATE!” The poem was likely influenced by Johnson’s time in the Navy, and it makes the apt argument that the state creates conditions wherein racialized and queer people subjugate themselves in service to it. This is the project of respectability politics: it situates marginalized bodies as “problems” so that they enact a form of self-censure in an attempt to become exemplary citizens. It is, in other words, a type of S/M over Black life.

The turn to S/M is a way out from those respectable restraints, as McClodden says: “Engaging within BDSM can allow one to experience violence that may feel imminent before it happens . . . I realized years ago that I could satisfy these urges with my own hand, through S/M, as a Black queer woman. I was interested in consensual pain as a form of tenderizing, or softness, or something that is of the interior self.” For individuals who have experienced destructive sadism in their lives (either at the hands of the state or in interpersonal contexts), S/M offers sites to transform embodied fear into something else that allows them to move past the moment of violence. The reality is that we are all capable of harming others, and we often do so with little or no harmful intent—just simple carelessness. Witnessing someone hold space and perform aftercare for someone they are physically harming troubles our senses and our binary understanding of perpetrators and sufferers. Seeing tender embraces of violence allows us to grasp what breaches of this dynamic look like. It is conflict held with care.

Such works are often described using the neoliberal platitudes of reclaiming, recovery, or healing that obscure the more unknown affective registers of our experiences of both the body and cinema. These directors render time as something felt rather than measured or controlled. By resisting the claim of healing that desires to “complete” the body or restore it, Madsen and McClodden make us complicit voyeurs in their desire to see what becomes of themselves, as filmmakers, and their audiences when acts of exigent sadism are pursued. The final moments of McClodden’s “On Subjugation” segment show her panting and heaving as she struggles to finish the poem before the tape runs out; she is approaching a state of jouissance both physically and aesthetically by completing the poem in time. Likewise, in A Body to Live In , Musafar and DuBois bond with Grindatti by sharing with him the temporal state of pain they’re inflicting on him. This, to me, is what a cinema of devotion feels like—a cinema that, by inviting us to share time tenderly and caringly with others enduring pain, allows us to touch the unknown within ourselves.

title_zh: 【坂本龍一｜觀音・聽時】他在藍色的地平線上，看見群風的歌與歷史的天使──「坂本龍一｜觀音・聽時」展覽側記
summary_zh: 来源摘录：坂本龍一認為音樂既是時間的藝術、僅存於時間之中，卻又同時對西方世界的單一線性時間感到存疑，於是我們可以想像，「坂本龍一｜觀音・聽時」展覽既是他對時間的提問，同時也是他在有限的生命時間裡，對時間的回應。——歷史是什麼？歷史就是天使，向後吹向未來。歷史是殘骸的山，天使自此追溯到過去。 這篇文章 【坂本龍一｜觀音・聽時】他在藍色的地平線上，看見群風的歌與歷史的天使──「坂本龍一｜觀音・聽時」展覽側記 最早出現於 釀電影 。

article_text:
Glasgow’s Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum removed an ancient Egyptian mummified head from view because there was no “informed consent from the deceased individual,” the museum said. The move has upset some conservative politicians in Scotland, with one alleging that it is a sign of “woke madness.”

According to the Times of London , the museum had previously displayed the mummified male head in its galleries. But it has now been moved to storage, and in its place is a notice reading: “We have removed human remains from this display as a mark of respect.”

A museum spokesperson sent the Times a statement that referred to industry guidelines recommended by the International Council of Museums. That group urges institutions displaying human remains to do so with “respect,” and states in its guidelines , “In all cases where human remains hold continuing cultural or spiritual importance, museums should consider restricted use or repatriation as appropriate.”

Per the Times , the museum also removed the remains of a priest, a mummified hand from Luxor, and a mummified foot.

Many European and American museums, from the Louvre to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, continue to display mummified people in their galleries. But some institutions have begun to change how they show these remains.

In the case of the National Museums of Scotland, for example, the institutions avoid using the term “mummy” in didactics, instead utilizing phrases such as “mummified person” and “mummified remains.” Doing so, the museums said in 2023, is an effort to avoid “dehumanizing” language .

A Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum spokesperson this week framed its removal of mummified remains within the context of consent. “In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals,” the museum told the Times .

At least one conservative politician has weighed in on the situation. Murdo Fraser, the former deputy leader of the Scottish Conservatives and a current MSP, told the Times , “Even Egyptian mummies are now being cancelled by a society so obsessed with modern sensibilities that it has lost all sense of perspective. People visit museums to learn about ancient civilisations, not to see history hidden away because it fails to meet today’s ideological standards.”

He called the development a sign of “woke madness,” a sentiment that was echoed in some corners of X.

“Fuck off. Just fuck off with this brainless shit,” reads one X repost of the Daily Mail article about the news. It has more than 7,000 likes.
excerpt_original: The museum cited a lack of “informed consent from the deceased individual” as its reasoning. One politician mocked the move as “woke madness.”

article_text:
対話を通してルーヴル美術館展を深める

国立新美術館（東京・六本木）で開催中の「ルーヴル美術館展 ルネサンス」の見どころや、美術史的背景、作家についてなどをわかりやすく解説する公開講座「対話で楽しむ『ルーヴル美術館展 ルネサンス』」が11月4日(水)と22日(日)に、よみうりカルチャー北千住（北千住駅ビル・ルミネ９階）で開催されます。受講者を募集しています。

アートナビゲーターの深津優希さんが講師を務め、講座参加者との対話を通して鑑賞体験を深めるとともに、展覧会を楽しむためのヒントを示してくれます。

「ルーヴル美術展展 ルネサンス」は12月13日まで

「ルーヴル美術館展 ルネサンス」は国立新美術館で12月13日（日）までの開催。レオナルド・ダ・ヴィンチの《女性の肖像》、誤って付された別称《美しきフェロニエール》など、選び抜かれた56点の作品を通じて、ルネサンス美術に光を当てます。

対話で楽しむ「ルーヴル美術館展 ルネサンス」

【開催日時】 ▶11月 4日（水）19:00～20:30 ▶11月22日（日）10:30～12:00

【会場】 ▶よみうりカルチャー北千住 (北千住駅ビル・ルミネ９階)

【参加費】 ▶4,510円（よみうりカルチャー会員3,960円）

article_text:
A s a kid in 90s Birmingham , Keiran Goddard would gather with his friends to watch the tower blocks coming down. That’s what passed for entertainment back then. Controlled explosions, collapsing buildings. The demolition of the city’s postwar council estates marked the end of one story and the start of another. It was a dust-blown display of regeneration and progress. The housing that replaced it would be an improvement. The people of east Birmingham would move on to better lives.

Goddard, specifically, moved on to study English at Oxford University. He now lives in London and writes books for a living. Physically, he has left his home town far behind. Emotionally and spiritually, not so much. “So I feel quite splintered,” he says. “I’m not sure anyone ever really leaves the world they grew up in.”

Goddard’s Birmingham-set second novel has just been made into a film. Enda Walsh wrote the script; Clio Barnard called the shots. Set in and around an anonymous housing estate, I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is a jolting, stirring ensemble drama in which a tower block’s demolition serves as a kind of societal big bang, spinning five childhood friends into a fraught adulthood.

When writing the book, Goddard identified with the character of Patrick, the idealistic graduate turned zero hours delivery driver who argues that decent housing is a basic human right, not a capital asset. But he’s also like Rian, the group’s breakout star, who made a killing on the stock market and bought a sterile London flat. Rian is the chief investor behind a new apartment complex that is to be built on the bones of the old estate. The film shows it rising in time-lapse leaps and bounds, just as historic strains set to work on Rian’s close-knit gang of mates.

The story scaffold may be simple, yet the drama that follows is anything but. It’s nuanced, thorny and possibly irresolvable, with no easy answers or obvious hero to root for. Goddard wrote the book as a series of interior monologues then delivered it to his agent and editor in a spirit of wild optimism. “I said, ‘You know, I think it’s got some cinematic potential.’ And both of them replied, saying, ‘There’s no dialogue and not much happens. It’s got the least cinematic potential of anything that we’ve seen.’”

The film was a challenge, Barnard admits. It’s about the pull of the past and the sharp edge of the present, stitching an intimate human story against the broader social canvas. “It feels to me that there is an equality in this group of friends,” the director says. “And that the antagonist is the system, which is a hard thing to represent.” She was fired up, however, by its brand of political rage and its fine-grained depiction of an embattled working-class community. “Also, it made me laugh,” she adds. Shared jokes are the glue of all successful friendship groups. Rian’s mates mock his lifestyle – his posh girlfriend and big fridge – but they are ruefully, lovingly pleased for him, too.

Barnard has always been drawn to the margins of the UK. She likes outsiders, pariahs, survivors and scamps. She made an eye-catching debut with 2010’s The Arbor , a brilliant lip-synced documentary about the Bradford-born playwright Andrea Dunbar, who died of a brain haemorrhage at the age of 29. The Selfish Giant was arguably harsher still: a devastating coming-of-age drama, foraging for scrap metal on the tatty fringes of town. One hesitates to say that she has since lightened up. All the same, 2021’s Ali & Ava – an interracial love story, as tender as a bruise – and I See Buildings at least come with an air of hard-won optimism.

“I think that’s been a conscious choice,” she says. “With Ali & Ava, I wanted the audience to leave with the feeling that they were able to act. And what I got from the group of people in this film was a massive amount of compassion and hope. I see a lot of Keiran in [the character of] Patrick. And Patrick’s a hopeful person. He believes that political change is still possible.”

The world has now slipped seriously out of whack, she admits. “Just look at the protests in France at the moment. There’s an economic imbalance everywhere. It’s hard to find a regular income and a roof over your head, especially for young people. But hope in itself can be an active resistance. Joy in itself can be its own positive protest.”

As for the film industry, that’s arguably out of whack, too. I See Buildings lands in the UK fresh from a triumphant unveiling at the Cannes film festival. The international critics adored it. The Guardian’s own Peter Bradshaw gave it a five-star review . But Barnard’s film might also prove to be among the last of a dying breed. It’s a blast of impassioned old-school social realism, folded in amid a glut of studio sequels and mythic heroes’ journeys, crying out to an audience that may no longer exist.

Goddard begs to differ. Like Patrick, he has hope; he puts his faith in the people. “We’ve seen it in publishing where the types of issues – the economic precarity – that traditionally affected only working-class communities are creeping more into middle-class society,” he says. “That means there’s a greater middle-class appetite for these kinds of stories. ‘Oh, you know that thing you’ve been moaning about for years? Well, it’s happening to me now as well.’” On the most basic level, he adds, the maths doesn’t add up. “The fact that the lives that are most frequently lived are the ones that are least frequently depicted. Economically, that’s stupid. You can’t simultaneously hold the view that people want to relate to stories and that the stories about the most common lives just aren’t viable. Those two things cannot be true. They can’t coexist.”

Probably every human life is one of explosions and upheaval, and it can take a while for the dust to settle. Nowadays, Goddard has a clearer view of who he is and where he came from. He is a product, he says, of Blair-era social mobility: the beneficiary of a fleeting, fitful period of wealth redistribution. He was told that if he worked hard and behaved he might one day, God willing, rise out of his class. “That was always the story,” he says. “To succeed meant to leave.”

In I See Buildings, Rian (played by Peaky Blinders star Joe Cole) winds up as a square peg in his fancy London apartment, pining for the streets, pubs and friends that he has left behind. Goddard can relate. “I’ve been very lucky. I’m not the victim here. As far as there is a right side of the equation to be on, I’m on it. The structures that enabled me to be here no longer exist. If you ran my life again now, it wouldn’t be the same. But yes, I think it does cause problems. You’re never truly accepted, and you can never properly go home. So you end up as a ghost, haunting the edges of two lives.”

A film of his book could have been a disaster, he knows. “There are a number of different flavours of wrong,” he says. It might have wound up as poverty porn, or an earnest slab of liberal doggerel. It might have involved flat caps and misery, or poured out eight pints of mindless, bleary-eyed hedonism. Instead, he thinks that Walsh and Barnard have improved on his work. They’ve made the tale funnier, more rousing and hopeful.

Best of all, Barnard filmed it on the streets of Birmingham. Goddard’s brother Tom helped integrate the crew with the community. The Crown social club served as the chief base of operations, where an open casting call drew as many as 800 local people. In a traditional story arc, the wayfaring hero eventually returns home. Odysseus arrives at Ithaca. Dorothy wakes up in her cosy Kansas farmhouse. The social mobility kids, Goddard feels, have been denied their third act. It’s the price they must pay for all the advances they’ve made. “But there was something very moving about going through this whole journey and literally returning to the estate I grew up on,” he says. “That was beyond special. That doesn’t normally happen. It’s as though, out of nowhere, I’ve been gifted the rare opportunity to close the circle and go home.”

I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is in cinemas on 4 December

title_original: The Aging Artist
editorial_excerpt_zh: 再来一次？：《杰·凯利》、《迟来的名气》与《麦克风开着吗？》探讨了它们的创作者是否还有继续下去的精力和动力
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "我还能再做一次吗？我还能再拍一部电影、演一出戏剧、写另一首诗或另一部歌剧吗？这就是日渐衰老的艺术家的困境：他们还能找到字句、精力和继续下去的动力吗？如果不能，这位艺术家还能在没有这种对其生存乃至核心身份至关重要的实践的情况下生活吗？或者说，这种实践真的那么核心吗？我的任务是为刚刚落幕的纽约电影节撰文评述三部隐晦或明了地提出这些问题的电影——《迟来的名气》、《杰·凯利》和《麦克风开着吗？》。但真正的挑战或许在于，找出阵容中哪些电影没有提出这些问题。在约阿希姆·特里尔（Joachim Trier）的《感伤价值》（Sentimental Value）中，斯特兰·斯卡斯加德（Stellan Skarsgård）极度渴望再拍一部电影，这部电影关乎家族历史，并希望由他疏远的女儿（由雷娜特·赖因斯维[Renate Reinsve]饰演）主演。在彼得罗·马切利（Pietro Marcello）的《杜丝》（Duse）中，瓦莱里亚·布鲁尼·泰德斯基（Valeria Bruni Tedeschi）饰演的这位痴迷而耀眼的歌剧名伶，即便与日渐衰弱的身体对抗，也依然紧抓着延续职业生涯的希望。伊桑·霍克（Ethan Hawke）饰演的《蓝月亮》（Blue Moon）中酗酒的歌词作家洛伦兹·哈特（Lorenz Hart），在被理查德·罗杰斯（Richard Rodgers）抛弃并转而选择奥斯卡·汉默斯坦二世（Oscar Hammerstein II）之后，陷入了生涯晚期的痛苦之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有时，年轻的艺术家与年长的自己仿佛是两个人，彼此争论不休。肯特·琼斯（Kent Jones）执导的《迟来的名气》中的威廉·达福（Willem Dafoe）所饰演的昔日诗人埃德·萨克斯伯格（Ed Saxberger），正是这种情况。很难想象在这部由萨米·伯奇（Samy Burch，2023年电影《五月的你，十二月的她》的编剧）改编自阿瑟·施尼茨勒（Arthur Schnitzler）惊艳中篇小说的忧郁电影中，还有谁能成为这个深思熟虑、真挚动人的核心。萨克斯伯格在几十年前下城波希米亚主义的创作高潮期出版过一本诗集，如今他靠做邮政工人分拣信件度日，并在廉价酒吧里与一帮银发蓝领工人厮混（可以想象成没有教职和持续诗歌创作的布考斯韦尔式人物）。他作为作家的生活几乎已被遗忘，直到一次偶然的相遇威胁着——或者说许诺着——去复苏它。一天傍晚，一个年轻的崇拜者、一个名叫迈尔斯（Edmund Donovan）的年轻诗人，在街上接近了他。迈尔斯最近发现了萨克斯伯格的书，他羞怯而又满怀热情地力劝萨克斯伯格去见见他那个由乳臭未干的业余艺术家和作家圈子里的其他书迷，他们自称为“热情社”。这位年长的男子或许愿意参与他们的一次朗诵会，并为这个场合写一首原创诗歌？（这里有一个意料之中的圈套：迈尔斯当然希望萨克斯伯格来朗诵并点评——即赞美——他自己的诗歌努力。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一天晚上，萨克斯伯格按时来到咖啡馆，并被介绍认识了全男班的“热情社”成员。稍后到来并带着一丝戏剧感的是格洛丽亚（格蕾塔·李[Greta Lee]），一位中年女演员，她在群体中的角色是……什么？吉祥物、灵感女神、跟屁虫？任君挑选——或者说也许这三者皆是。在书中她也是一个奇怪的角色，为了迎合每个男人和她自己的目的而改变个性，宛如情欲中的一粒沙砾。一个更具现代感的转折或许会让群里出现一个真正的女作家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“热情社”以坚守过时的正直理念而自豪。他们拒绝科技，并嘲笑邻桌的竞争对手为在互联网上自我推广的“网红”。他们在片头字幕期间伴随着梦幻般的历史素材和背景音乐所展现的自身模范，是早期波希米亚主义的融合体：纽约画派（那个由不同信念、垮掉派和形式主义者、呼喊与低语组成的形形色色的艺术家和作家联盟）——与更近的过去、一个以影迷文化为标志的60年代末和70年代自由放纵的纽约相交织，证据就是萨克斯伯格书架上隐约可见的电影书籍。（是的，亲爱的读者，当年商业出版物确实在出版影评人撰写的文集。而且人们也确实在阅读它们！）电影评论家的崛起显然没有引起“热情社”成员的注意；其中一人自我介绍说是评论家，然后立刻纠正自己——“散文家！”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这部施尼茨勒的中篇小说中，评论家以身为评论家而自豪，但将自己与“书评人”区分开来。这只是作者众多敏锐观察之一，他对波希米亚附庸风雅者的轻度讽刺画像（维也纳背景在电影中被替换为纽约）是如此现代，以至于显得不可思议。（施尼茨勒曾为多部电影提供原创故事，包括《大开眼戒》和绝妙的《轮舞》。）这位作者世纪之交的维也纳职业生涯追随者与我们21世纪纽约的追随者几乎没有区别，因此剧本几乎无需改动。一个精明的当代增补是，这群自豪地特立独行的文人背后有信托基金支撑，并且乐于同出版业的人打交道，后者想让萨克斯伯格写回忆录——并承诺提供枪手代笔，还大谈“影响力”、“创意人士”和“内容”。然而，我们是否会相信萨克斯伯格70年代的那个圈子就没那么荒谬、更具英雄主义呢？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影不可避免地失去的是一种语调的一致性，即当萨克斯伯格在脑海中来回踱步、试图寻找词句来创作一首诗却以失败告终、最终在朗诵会上定下一首旧诗时，他自己也成为了他的虚荣心的笑柄。那种摆脱羞耻感与失败感、以及摆脱与年轻作家之间虚假联系的解脱，来自于一个光辉而具有宣泄意义的结局，它直接取自那部中篇小说——与其中一位作家的对唱，在这段对唱中，显现出无论是他还是小组成员的其他任何人，都没有读过萨克斯伯格的一个字。“我们做个交易吧，”他向这个年轻男子建议道，“你不需要读我的诗，作为交换，我也不读你的——好吗？”阿门。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "乔治·克鲁尼（George Clooney）在诺亚·鲍姆巴赫（Noah Baumbach）的《杰伊·凯利》（Jay Kelly）中饰演同名演员——一个行将退场、身处迟暮的“老派电影明星最后一人”，同时也是个糟糕的父亲（他的两个女儿是极具挑战性的存在）。克鲁尼统领着一群阿谀奉承的随从，这支如离心力般旋转的演员阵容最终陪着他一同游历欧洲——一个贴切的类比是《八部半》（8½）。然而，尽管克鲁尼或许具备马斯楚安尼（Mastroianni）表面的磁场，却全无那种让这场无处可去的马戏团带上一丝厚重感的倦世之感、徒劳感甚至是自我厌恶。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最有趣的，是凯利与他全天候24/7的经纪人（由极具吸引力的亚当·桑德勒饰演）之间，那种鲜明且愈发尴尬、回荡着紧迫感的问题：这种本质上不平等、类似于主仆的关系，是否能演变成真正的友情？如果不能，又该会如何让人心生芥蒂？劳拉·邓恩（Laura Dern）饰演的公关兼桑德勒的前女友同样表现极佳。至于那位“日渐衰老”的艺术家，克鲁尼/凯利极力证明自己并非行将就木，而是正处于矫健敏捷的中年状态，他一次又一次地找借口，身手敏捷、如风般奔跑穿梭于各个地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布莱德利·库珀（Bradley Cooper）的《这个在运作吗？》（Is This Thing On?）中的威尔·阿奈特（Will Arnett）与其说是一个日渐衰老的艺术家，不如说是一个苦苦挣扎、过着朝九晚五（9-to-5）生活的失意中年人，却意外发现了自己作为艺术家的潜质。他正处于离婚的边缘，劳拉·邓恩再次以生动且极具说服力的表演饰演他的妻子。一天夜里，他在纽约西村（West Village）闲逛时发现，要想在某家酒吧喝上一杯免费饮品，就必须在地下室的开放麦（open mic）上即兴表演一番。他的表现并不算出彩，但在观看其他单口喜剧演员的表演时，他被他们的快乐、幽默和情谊深深吸引了。他坚持了下来并渐入佳境，发现通过在舞台上宣泄恶魔来获得自由，比任何离婚治疗都更有效。通过自白式的俏皮短句，他在晚年发现了一种新的身份——化身单口喜剧演员的回忆录作家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿奈特本人发现了英国喜剧演员约翰·比什（John Bishop）的起源故事，并将其带给了老朋友库珀。这位从演员转型为导演的创作者不仅抓住了两个分居伴侣之间的浪漫，还捕捉到了两个纽约的交织——充满粗粝感的下城喜剧俱乐部与一尘不染、绿树成荫的郊区。他对孩子们的刻画也很出色（布莱克·凯恩 [Blake Kane] 与卡尔文·克内格滕 [Calvin Knegten] 饰演这对分居夫妇的儿子），即便在危机时刻，这部电影也带有一种充满活力、玩世不恭的氛围。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着妻子和丈夫的争执与交谈，他们发现，他们所感受到的空虚，更多源于他们在婚姻中曾经或是已经变成的那种人，而非婚姻本身。有时这部电影类似于鲍姆巴赫的《婚姻故事》（Marriage Story，邓恩在其中饰演了一名离婚律师）：片中某一刻，身为家庭理发师的邓恩为她的前夫理发，呼应了2019年那部电影中的相似场景。不同之处在于，这里两个个体之间存在着一种对等关系，这与《婚姻故事》中的丈夫和妻子形成对比：亚当·司提夫（Adam Driver）饰演充满激情且成功的艺术家，而斯嘉丽·约翰逊（Scarlett Johansson）则饰演好莱坞事业平平的家庭主妇。在《这个在运作吗？》中，陷入泥潭的不止阿奈特一人；邓恩的角色曾是一名光鲜亮丽、意气风发的奥运会排球运动员，为了母亲的角色而放弃了事业，而如今，令她懊恼的是，她不得不晋升（在她看来是降格）为教练的角色。不再有动作戏。这是在适时需要拥抱的又一个身份。同样令人着迷的是，邓恩在展现和诠释一个中年女性时所流露出的优雅。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "归根结底，这是一部关于婚姻作为一种悖论的电影。婚姻可能吗？不能。离婚可能吗？不见得，或者说无法彻底做到。我们生活在一个对婚姻施加前所未有巨大压力的世界里。我们渴望平等，但总得有人操持家务；我们在追求个人成长，哪怕我们活得更久、超越了过去的自己。这会让你陷入重重纠葛。它也可以极大地肯定生命，而孩子们正是这个方程的一部分。这不是什么石破天惊的启示，但库珀让它显得自然而然，甚至熠熠生辉。这是一部让人感觉良好的电影，却并非头脑简单。对于片中的年迈角色而言，即便不是为了我们所有的主角，去创造或偶然发现一个新的自我，并协商建立一段温馨且持久的关系，也永远都不会太迟。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Can I do it again? Can I make another film, act in another play, write another poem or libretto? This is the quandary of the aging artist: can they find the words, the energy, the motivation to continue? And if not, can said artist live without the practice so central to their being, to their very identity? Or is it so central? My mandate was to write on three films at the just-ended New York Film Festival that, implicitly or explicitly, raise these questions— Late Fame , Jay Kelly , and Is This Thing On? But the real challenge might have been to identify which films from the lineup don’t ask these questions. In Joachim Trier’s Sentimental Value , Stellan Skarsgård wants desperately to make one more film, this one about family history and hopefully starring his estranged daughter, played by Renate Reinsve. In Pietro Marcello’s Duse , Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s obsessed and glittering diva clings to hopes of continuing her career even as she battles an ailing body. Blue Moon ’s alcoholic lyricist Lorenz Hart, played by Ethan Hawke, finds himself in late-career agony after having been ditched by Richard Rodgers in favor of Oscar Hammerstein II."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sometimes it’s as if the young artist and his older self are two different people, arguing with each other. This is precisely the case with Ed Saxberger, the onetime poet played by Willem Dafoe in Kent Jones’s Late Fame. It’s hard to imagine anyone else at the thoughtful, heartfelt center of this melancholy film, adapted from a stunning Arthur Schnitzler novella by Samy Burch (the screenwriter of 2023’s May December ). Saxberger, who published one book of poetry decades ago, in the creative surge of a downtown New York bohemia, now sorts letters as a postal worker and hangs out at dive bars with fellow silver-haired blue-collar workers (think Bukowski without the teaching gigs and continuous production of poetry). His life as a writer is all but forgotten until a chance encounter threatens—or promises—to revive it. One evening, a young admirer, an aspiring poet named Meyers (Edmund Donovan), approaches him on the street. Having recently discovered Saxberger’s book, Meyers shyly but fulsomely urges him to come and meet other fans among his coterie of callow wannabe artists and writers, who call themselves “The Enthusiasm Society.” Perhaps the older man would like to participate in one of their readings, and write an original poem for the occasion? (There’s a predictable catch: Meyers of course wants Saxberger to read and critique—i.e., praise—his own poetic efforts.)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Saxberger duly arrives at the coffeehouse one evening, and is introduced to the all-male Enthusiasts. Arriving later, and bringing an air of theatricality, is Gloria (Greta Lee), a middle-aged actress, whose role in the group is… what? Mascot, muse, hanger-on? Take your pick—or maybe it’s all three. She’s a strange creature in the book as well, altering her personality to suit each man and her purpose, a bit of gravel in the eros. A more contemporary twist might have had an actual woman writer in the group."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Enthusiasts pride themselves on staying true to an old-fashioned idea of integrity. They reject technology and ridicule competitors at a neighboring table as “influencers” who promote themselves on the internet. Their own model, imagined in dreamlike period footage and background music during the opening credits, is an amalgam of earlier bohemias: the New York School, that motley coalition of artists and writers of different persuasions, Beats and formalists, howling and whispering—meshed with a more recent past, a late-’60s and ’70s free-for-all New York marked by cinephilia, the proof being the movie books glimpsed on Saxberger’s shelf. (Yes, dear reader, back in the day trade publishers were actually putting out anthologies of writing by film critics. And people were reading them!) The ascendancy of the movie critic has apparently escaped the notice of the Enthusiasts; one introduces himself as a critic and then immediately corrects himself—“essayist!”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the Schnitzler novella, the critic is proud to be one, but distinguishes himself from “reviewers.” This is just one of the sharp observations of the author, whose lightly satirical portrait of bohemian poseurs (in Vienna, replaced by New York in the movie) is so modern as to seem uncanny. (Schnitzler has furnished original stories for a number of films, including Eyes Wide Shut and the magnificent La Ronde .) The author’s turn-of-the-century Viennese careerists differ so very little from ours of 21st-century New York that there was little to change in the script. One astute contemporary addition is that these proudly off-the-beaten-path litterateurs are backed by trust funds and happily deal with members of the publishing industry who want Saxberger to write his memoirs—with a ghostwriter to be provided, and talk of “impact,” “creatives,” and “content.” Yet are we to believe that Saxberger’s ’70s coterie was any less ridiculous, any more heroic?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What the film inevitably loses is a tonal consistency, the sense that Saxberger too is the butt of his vanity as he goes back and forth in his head, trying to find words to create a poem, failing, eventually settling on an old poem for the reading. Release from a sense of shame and failure, and from his pseudo-connection with the young writers, comes in a gloriously cathartic ending, straight out of the novella—a duet with one of the writers in which it becomes apparent that neither he nor the rest of the group has read a word of Saxberger’s. “Let’s make a deal,” he suggests to the young man. “You don’t need to read my poems, and in exchange, I won’t read yours either—all right?” Amen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "George Clooney plays the eponymous actor in Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly , “the last of the old movie stars” on his way out, an aging man who’s also a bad dad (his two daughters are challenging presences). Clooney presides over an ensemble of hangers-on, a swirling centrifugal cast that ends up traveling with him through Europe—an apt comparison is 8½. But while Clooney may have some of the surface magnetism of Mastroianni, there’s none of the world-weariness, the sense of futility or even self-disgust, that gave a touch of gravitas to the circus going nowhere."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Most interesting is the stark and increasingly awkward question that resounds with urgency between Kelly and his 24/7 manager, played by a riveting Adam Sandler: can such an inherently unequal relationship, akin to master and slave, ever evolve into friendship? And how, if not, must that rankle? Also terrific is Laura Dern as his publicist and Sandler’s ex-lover. As for the “aging” artist, Clooney/Kelly goes out of his way to prove he’s not on his last legs but on very spry middle-aged ones, as he scampers and runs like the wind over one territory after another, with one excuse after another."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Will Arnett in Bradley Cooper’s Is This Thing On? can’t be considered an aging artist so much as a flailing, middle-aged 9-to-5er who finds himself as an artist. He’s on the verge of divorce, with Laura Dern again vivid and persuasive as his wife. One night, wandering around New York’s West Village, he finds that to get a free drink at a certain bar he must do a bit of improv at the open mic in the basement. He’s not very good, but watching the other stand-ups, he becomes enthralled by their joy and humor and camaraderie. He persists and gradually improves, finding that the freedom to exorcise his demons on stage is much more effective than any divorce therapy. Through confessional one-liners, he discovers late in life a new identity—the memoirist as stand-up comic."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arnett himself discovered the origin story of British comedian John Bishop, and brought it to longtime friend Cooper. The actor-turned-director seized on the romance not just of two separating partners but also of two New Yorks—the seedier downtown of comedy clubs vs. the pristinely leafy suburbs. He’s good with the children, too (Blake Kane and Calvin Knegten play the estranged couple’s sons), and even at moments of crisis the movie has a spirited, playful feel."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As the wife and husband tussle and talk, they discover that the emptiness they felt was more about who they were or had become within the marriage than the marriage itself. There are times when the film resembles Baumbach’s Marriage Story (in which Dern played a divorce lawyer): at one point Dern, the family barber, cuts her ex’s hair, echoing a similar scene in the 2019 film. The difference is that there’s an equivalence between the two people here, as opposed to the husband and wife in Marriage Story : Adam Driver’s passionate and successful artist vs. Scarlett Johansson’s homemaker with an iffy Hollywood career. In Is This Thing On? , Arnett is not the only one stuck in a rut; Dern’s character was an Olympic volleyball player with glamour and swagger who left her career for motherhood, and now, to her chagrin, must graduate (or descend, in her mind) to the role of coach. No more action. Another identity to embrace in due course. What’s no less compelling is the grace with which Dern plays and looks like a woman in middle age."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ultimately this is a film about marriage as a paradox. Is marriage possible? No. Is divorce possible? Not really, or not definitively. We live in a world where there are greater pressures on marriage than ever. We want equality but somebody’s got to manage the home; we want individual growth even as we live longer and outgrow earlier selves. It can tie you up in knots. article_text:
Can I do it again? Can I make another film, act in another play, write another poem or libretto? This is the quandary of the aging artist: can they find the words, the energy, the motivation to continue? And if not, can said artist live without the practice so central to their being, to their very identity? Or is it so central? My mandate was to write on three films at the just-ended New York Film Festival that, implicitly or explicitly, raise these questions— Late Fame , Jay Kelly , and Is This Thing On? But the real challenge might have been to identify which films from the lineup don’t ask these questions. In Joachim Trier’s Sentimental Value , Stellan Skarsgård wants desperately to make one more film, this one about family history and hopefully starring his estranged daughter, played by Renate Reinsve. In Pietro Marcello’s Duse , Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s obsessed and glittering diva clings to hopes of continuing her career even as she battles an ailing body. Blue Moon ’s alcoholic lyricist Lorenz Hart, played by Ethan Hawke, finds himself in late-career agony after having been ditched by Richard Rodgers in favor of Oscar Hammerstein II.

Sometimes it’s as if the young artist and his older self are two different people, arguing with each other. This is precisely the case with Ed Saxberger, the onetime poet played by Willem Dafoe in Kent Jones’s Late Fame. It’s hard to imagine anyone else at the thoughtful, heartfelt center of this melancholy film, adapted from a stunning Arthur Schnitzler novella by Samy Burch (the screenwriter of 2023’s May December ). Saxberger, who published one book of poetry decades ago, in the creative surge of a downtown New York bohemia, now sorts letters as a postal worker and hangs out at dive bars with fellow silver-haired blue-collar workers (think Bukowski without the teaching gigs and continuous production of poetry). His life as a writer is all but forgotten until a chance encounter threatens—or promises—to revive it. One evening, a young admirer, an aspiring poet named Meyers (Edmund Donovan), approaches him on the street. Having recently discovered Saxberger’s book, Meyers shyly but fulsomely urges him to come and meet other fans among his coterie of callow wannabe artists and writers, who call themselves “The Enthusiasm Society.” Perhaps the older man would like to participate in one of their readings, and write an original poem for the occasion? (There’s a predictable catch: Meyers of course wants Saxberger to read and critique—i.e., praise—his own poetic efforts.)

Saxberger duly arrives at the coffeehouse one evening, and is introduced to the all-male Enthusiasts. Arriving later, and bringing an air of theatricality, is Gloria (Greta Lee), a middle-aged actress, whose role in the group is… what? Mascot, muse, hanger-on? Take your pick—or maybe it’s all three. She’s a strange creature in the book as well, altering her personality to suit each man and her purpose, a bit of gravel in the eros. A more contemporary twist might have had an actual woman writer in the group.

The Enthusiasts pride themselves on staying true to an old-fashioned idea of integrity. They reject technology and ridicule competitors at a neighboring table as “influencers” who promote themselves on the internet. Their own model, imagined in dreamlike period footage and background music during the opening credits, is an amalgam of earlier bohemias: the New York School, that motley coalition of artists and writers of different persuasions, Beats and formalists, howling and whispering—meshed with a more recent past, a late-’60s and ’70s free-for-all New York marked by cinephilia, the proof being the movie books glimpsed on Saxberger’s shelf. (Yes, dear reader, back in the day trade publishers were actually putting out anthologies of writing by film critics. And people were reading them!) The ascendancy of the movie critic has apparently escaped the notice of the Enthusiasts; one introduces himself as a critic and then immediately corrects himself—“essayist!”

In the Schnitzler novella, the critic is proud to be one, but distinguishes himself from “reviewers.” This is just one of the sharp observations of the author, whose lightly satirical portrait of bohemian poseurs (in Vienna, replaced by New York in the movie) is so modern as to seem uncanny. (Schnitzler has furnished original stories for a number of films, including Eyes Wide Shut and the magnificent La Ronde .) The author’s turn-of-the-century Viennese careerists differ so very little from ours of 21st-century New York that there was little to change in the script. One astute contemporary addition is that these proudly off-the-beaten-path litterateurs are backed by trust funds and happily deal with members of the publishing industry who want Saxberger to write his memoirs—with a ghostwriter to be provided, and talk of “impact,” “creatives,” and “content.” Yet are we to believe that Saxberger’s ’70s coterie was any less ridiculous, any more heroic?

What the film inevitably loses is a tonal consistency, the sense that Saxberger too is the butt of his vanity as he goes back and forth in his head, trying to find words to create a poem, failing, eventually settling on an old poem for the reading. Release from a sense of shame and failure, and from his pseudo-connection with the young writers, comes in a gloriously cathartic ending, straight out of the novella—a duet with one of the writers in which it becomes apparent that neither he nor the rest of the group has read a word of Saxberger’s. “Let’s make a deal,” he suggests to the young man. “You don’t need to read my poems, and in exchange, I won’t read yours either—all right?” Amen.

George Clooney plays the eponymous actor in Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly , “the last of the old movie stars” on his way out, an aging man who’s also a bad dad (his two daughters are challenging presences). Clooney presides over an ensemble of hangers-on, a swirling centrifugal cast that ends up traveling with him through Europe—an apt comparison is 8½. But while Clooney may have some of the surface magnetism of Mastroianni, there’s none of the world-weariness, the sense of futility or even self-disgust, that gave a touch of gravitas to the circus going nowhere.

Most interesting is the stark and increasingly awkward question that resounds with urgency between Kelly and his 24/7 manager, played by a riveting Adam Sandler: can such an inherently unequal relationship, akin to master and slave, ever evolve into friendship? And how, if not, must that rankle? Also terrific is Laura Dern as his publicist and Sandler’s ex-lover. As for the “aging” artist, Clooney/Kelly goes out of his way to prove he’s not on his last legs but on very spry middle-aged ones, as he scampers and runs like the wind over one territory after another, with one excuse after another.

Will Arnett in Bradley Cooper’s Is This Thing On? can’t be considered an aging artist so much as a flailing, middle-aged 9-to-5er who finds himself as an artist. He’s on the verge of divorce, with Laura Dern again vivid and persuasive as his wife. One night, wandering around New York’s West Village, he finds that to get a free drink at a certain bar he must do a bit of improv at the open mic in the basement. He’s not very good, but watching the other stand-ups, he becomes enthralled by their joy and humor and camaraderie. He persists and gradually improves, finding that the freedom to exorcise his demons on stage is much more effective than any divorce therapy. Through confessional one-liners, he discovers late in life a new identity—the memoirist as stand-up comic.

Arnett himself discovered the origin story of British comedian John Bishop, and brought it to longtime friend Cooper. The actor-turned-director seized on the romance not just of two separating partners but also of two New Yorks—the seedier downtown of comedy clubs vs. the pristinely leafy suburbs. He’s good with the children, too (Blake Kane and Calvin Knegten play the estranged couple’s sons), and even at moments of crisis the movie has a spirited, playful feel.

As the wife and husband tussle and talk, they discover that the emptiness they felt was more about who they were or had become within the marriage than the marriage itself. There are times when the film resembles Baumbach’s Marriage Story (in which Dern played a divorce lawyer): at one point Dern, the family barber, cuts her ex’s hair, echoing a similar scene in the 2019 film. The difference is that there’s an equivalence between the two people here, as opposed to the husband and wife in Marriage Story : Adam Driver’s passionate and successful artist vs. Scarlett Johansson’s homemaker with an iffy Hollywood career. In Is This Thing On? , Arnett is not the only one stuck in a rut; Dern’s character was an Olympic volleyball player with glamour and swagger who left her career for motherhood, and now, to her chagrin, must graduate (or descend, in her mind) to the role of coach. No more action. Another identity to embrace in due course. What’s no less compelling is the grace with which Dern plays and looks like a woman in middle age.

Ultimately this is a film about marriage as a paradox. Is marriage possible? No. Is divorce possible? Not really, or not definitively. We live in a world where there are greater pressures on marriage than ever. We want equality but somebody’s got to manage the home; we want individual growth even as we live longer and outgrow earlier selves. It can tie you up in knots. It can also be expansively life-affirming, and the children are part of the equation. It’s not a stop-the-presses revelation, but Cooper makes it feel organic, even incandescent. It’s a feel-good movie, but it’s not simpleminded. For the aging characters here, if not for all of our protagonists, it’s never too late to create or stumble upon a new self, and negotiate a welcoming and sustaining relationship.

横浜美術館で開催中の「マリー・アントワネット・スタイル 」の来場者が10月27日に30万人に到達して、記念セレモニーが行われました。開幕から休館日を除いて78日目の達成です。

マリー・アントワネット・スタイル

会期：2026年8月1日（土）～11月23日（月・祝）

会場：横浜美術館（神奈川県横浜市西区みなとみらい3-4-1）

開館時間：10時～18時（入館は閉館の30分前まで）、夜間開館日（11月2日、 7日、14日、20日、21日、22日）は20時まで延長

休館日：木曜日 ※11月19日は開館

アクセス：みなとみらい線「みなとみらい」駅から徒歩3分／JR（京浜東北・根岸線）・横浜市営地下鉄「桜木町」駅から徒歩10分

主催：横浜美術館、ヴィクトリア＆アルバート博物館、読売新聞社、日本テレビ放送網

特別協賛：キヤノン

協賛：DNP大日本印刷

後援：ブリティッシュ・カウンシル

きっかけは車内広告

記念の来場者となったのは、東京都世田谷区の女性です。電車内の広告が気になって検索したところ、ドレスなどの展示内容を知ったそうです。仕事が休みだったこの日、同僚を誘って来館しました。蔵屋美香館長から、記念に図録を贈られました。

「反感買う過程、いまのSNSのよう」

記念来場者の女性が横浜美術館を訪ねたのは、2018年のモネ展以来だそうです。「もともと世界史が好きでフランス革命にも興味がありましたし、マリー・アントワネットが市民の反感を買って、最後はギロチンにかけられたことは知っていた」と話しました。ソフィア・コッポラ監督の映画「マリー・アントワネット」（2006年）を見てファッションにも関心を持っていたのだとか。来館前に調べたところ、「市民の反感を買っていく過程で、今の時代のSNSのように実際と違う悪いイメージを植え付けられていったことがわかった」と語りました。

「セーヌ川は怖かったけど…」

女性は「パリに行ったときは、夜のセーヌ川でマリー・アントワネットが幽閉されていたシテ島の牢獄（コンシエルジュリー）を見て、怖いなと思いました」と思い出を語りました。一方で、同じ場所で行われた2024年のパリ・オリンピックの開会式で、マリー・アントワネットをモチーフにした赤いドレスの女性が生首を持って現れた演出を見て、「怖かったけどフランスっぽいアートだな」と理解できたそうです。

職業を聞いて納得

同僚の女性は「ヴェルサイユ宮殿も見に行ったことがあります。こんな感じの暮らしをしていたのかと思いましたが、いま、また見られるのは嬉しい」と話していました。興味のある展示を聞くと、二人は「ドレス、アクセサリー、髪形、歴史的資料」と次々に挙げてくれました。「髪形」というのが気になって、職業をお尋ねしたところ、「美容師です」と答えてくれたので納得しました。

◆11月には夜間開館日

取材は昼前に行いましたが、既に女性を中心に来場者の行列ができていました。人気ぶりを受けて、横浜美術館では11月の21、22日に設定していた夜間開館日を増やし、11月2日、7日、14日、20日にも追加しました。通常18時閉館のところ、20時まで開館します。入場は19時30分までです。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班・丸山謙一）
